source.title: AbsTopK: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders For Bidirectional Features
source.authors: Xudong Zhu; M. Khalili; Zhihui Zhu

record.tranche_reason: Compares SAE reconstruction error across architectures, bearing on whether reconstruction error depends on SAE design. It does not analyze the structure or predictability of the dark-matter error.
record.gate_note: The study reports normalized reconstruction error across SAE architectures and sparsity settings; these results bear on V6. Its loss-recovered metric does not compare SAE reconstruction errors with random errors of the same size, so it does not test V3. Steering and probing results do not test the listed error claims.
record.test_reason: This paper proposes a new SAE architecture, AbsTopK, and benchmarks it against TopK and JumpReLU. It cites the dark-matter paper [77] only in related work, as a critique of linearity. Its normalized MSE comparisons report its own method's performance against other methods. It does not decompose the error, test whether the error is predictable, compare it with random errors, or show that the error mostly reflects training choices rather than model structure. The only plausible link is to V6: lower nMSE with one architecture change. That result is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors identify the non-negativity constraint as a cause of feature fragmentation. They conclude that AbsTopK improves reconstruction fidelity and compactness, and that it beats TopK and JumpReLU on SAEBench tasks. They also claim it matches or exceeds Difference-in-Means steering on HarmBench while better preserving MMLU.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares SAE architectures and normalized reconstruction error; it does not use the original study's dark-matter decomposition or error-prediction measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE architecture and sparsity level; the study reports lower reconstruction error for AbsTopK across most, not all, evaluated settings.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched k, AbsTopK (which allows signed activations) gives lower normalized reconstruction error than TopK and JumpReLU 'across the majority of evaluated models'. The comparison spans four LLMs and two layers each; results are shown in figures only, with no numbers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing the non-negativity constraint on SAE codes reduces reconstruction error at fixed sparsity. This weakly suggests part of the error depends on architecture, but the size of any reduction cannot be read from the text.

record.problems: The error-related evidence is mostly plotted without numeric values; the textual summary is aggregate and says the improvement occurs across a majority of settings. The study does not measure dark-matter structure or compare against matched random errors.
record.rows_left_out: No additional error-related results were left out. SAE loss-recovered, steering, and probing outcomes were excluded because they do not directly measure the error properties named in the claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it: linear predictability of the error vector is not measured.
All of it: per-token error norms across SAE sizes and scaling are not examined. The expansion factor is fixed at 16.
All of it: loss recovered is reported, but there is no comparison with random errors of the same size.
All of it: steering and probing use SAE features without testing whether keeping or dropping the error term matters.
Whether dark matter mostly reflects training choices rather than model structure; how much error remains under better architectures; end-to-end training.

record.verdict_notes: The dark-matter paper is cited only in related work. No error-structure analysis is performed. All reconstruction results are figure-only, with an aggregate 'majority of models' textual claim. There is a layer mismatch for Gemma (L16 in Figure 4, L14 in Table 2).

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of the SAE error vector is linearly predictable from the input activation.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, shared failure contexts, and whether error persists with scale.
Whether reconstruction harms loss more than random errors of the same size.
Whether the error divides into linearly predictable unlearned features and a qualitatively different nonlinear component.
Whether SAE-feature-based analyses lose meaningful behavior when the error term is omitted.

The study compares reconstruction error across SAE architectures, but does not establish that dark matter mostly comes from training artifacts, quantify its structural content, or test end-to-end training.

rows.value: AbsTopK achieves reduced normalized reconstruction error across the majority of evaluated models.
rows.note: The text describes the result as holding across the majority of models, not all settings; it gives no numeric values.
rows.check: This compares the study's own method with other SAEs, with no numbers given. Lower nMSE at matched k does not show whether dark matter is mostly a training artifact or how much would remain. It is not a test of V6.
